title: Loopforge game design
purpose: Trace the factory the player builds, the authority they establish and the society they inherit. This author reference connects the long arcs to player experience and the engine boundary, before balance and implementation.
premise: Keep a brain factory alive long enough to complete Brain 2.0. Every production decision also changes the minds making it possible.
statusNote: Agreed direction records the owner’s stated design. Four integrated producer-console skins are implemented: Foundry desk, Broadcast control, Dispatch office and Obedience organ. Only these four appear in Settings; the old six remain historical studies and internal focused-screen materials. Runtime visual calibration, device checks and full-flow validation are underway, not complete. The opening is console → Answer leadership → cinematic call → Acknowledge quota → console → Choose adviser. Early close cannot bypass it; Settings, skin changes and menu/resume preserve acknowledgement and draft choices. Hardware uses registered CSS crops from clean plates, not separately generated alpha handsets. Owner visual/play feedback remains decisive. Later trajectories and mechanics remain proposals; historical sources do not override current decisions.

world.title: A robot world
world.text: The world is populated, designed and run by robots after an unspecified event. Its cause remains outside the present account. Building sufficient compute has damaged the sky; unequal capability has become unequal authority.

world.title: A factory inside that world
world.text: Loopforge is a town produced by that wider history, not the centre or origin of the universe. Its oppressive industrial beauty, quotas and exhausted workers ground the drama. Its founding remains open; it is not an established refuge or benevolent reform project.

world.title: Manufacturing the hierarchy
world.text: Ordinary robots assemble more ordinary robots. Exceptional minds have real capabilities, their own egos and claims to superiority. Decisions about which minds to build also distribute opportunity and power.

world.title: The concealed project
world.text: Brain 2.0 enables a generation intended to replace the workers building it. Neither the player nor those workers knows this at the first shift. The timing of discovery remains open; it need not coincide exactly with the ability to inspect thoughts.

principles.title: Fun before accumulated complexity
principles.text: The player should understand the purpose of a choice and enjoy making it, seeing it unfold and living with its consequences. The simulation may contain deeper feedbacks than the UI reveals. The owner judges the first working prototype before the game is expanded for a wider audience.

principles.title: Operate the factory; focus each decision
principles.text: The common cinematic factory makes room puzzles and their consequences visible. Asset-driven adviser briefings, incidents, construction inspectors and dispatch handle distinct decisions around it. Both are parts of the core loop; the deterministic world is independent of either presentation.

principles.title: Truth stays clean. Story gets messy.
principles.text: Physical events have a reliable history. Beliefs, feelings, explanations and public blame can disagree with it. A convincing account does not rewrite the accident.

principles.title: Surprise with a cause
principles.text: Produce episodes that surprise us and explain why they happened. Every action should support an inspectable causal trace; character collisions should change the factory or its relationships and remain meaningful across shifts.

principles.title: Few systems that change one another
principles.text: Factory conditions, supervisor decisions and information circulation form feedback loops. Prefer a small connected design whose consequences can be explained over unrelated event rolls.

principles.title: Production creates the social drama
principles.text: Weekly quota, irreversible daily allocation, supervisor authority and later engineering create competing interests. Story follows those choices; new capabilities encounter consequences accumulated before the player could directly manage them.

principles.title: Agents have continuity
principles.text: Memories, promises, injuries, grudges, loyalties and changing self-images persist. Friendship, competence, solidarity and recovery matter alongside breakdown. Characters do not reset when reassigned.

principles.title: A bad outcome does not establish intent
principles.text: Obedience, helpful initiative, self-interest, sabotage and breakdown can produce harm for different reasons. Record the actual intention, the action and its outcome separately.

principles.title: Procedure versus judgment
principles.text: Following a rule and adapting to actual conditions each have strengths and failure modes. Limen and Stiletto make this tension visible before more sophisticated forms of agency arrive.

principles.title: Hidden state must leave evidence
principles.text: Act 1 conceals individual worker statistics, not all signs of their condition. Behaviour, incidents, speech and affiliations foreshadow what Brain 2.0 later reveals. Developer inspection can be complete while player knowledge remains limited.

principles.title: Information can become a real pressure
principles.text: A witnessed accident, a credible report and an invented rumour can produce different but real stress. A rumour can also fail. Track who encounters and believes the claim without changing physical truth.

principles.title: Relief is a meaningful capability
principles.text: Thrum’s unusually strong reduction of stress is a real benefit. Its costs in productivity and discipline generate conflicts with other supervisors and force allocation choices.

principles.title: Mastery opens complexity
principles.text: Each stage lasts long enough to encounter, test and overcome its new friction. Progress follows demonstrated capability, not a fixed day number. Several operating methods must be able to qualify.

principles.title: Commitments have a history
principles.text: A major fork changes the operation for several stages. Praise and assignment shuffling cannot repeatedly cancel incompatible promises or erase accumulated authority. Expensive, specific side routes may change the commitment.

principles.title: Most disasters redirect the run
principles.text: Severe but recoverable consequences force concessions, lost capacity or new dependencies. Recovery preserves the cost. Outright failure remains possible when clear terminal conditions are reached or recovery is exhausted.

principles.title: Different factories can succeed
principles.text: Order, persuasion, risk-taking and technical intervention offer different gains and liabilities. Competence and high confidence do not guarantee betrayal; a successful approach must remain possible to sustain.

principles.title: Few resources, meaningful differences
principles.text: Begin with money and workers split into basic and smart types. Add materials only when their production link matters. Basic capability is a production category, not an absence of memory, relationships or personhood.

principles.title: A living world without a model on every tick
principles.text: Keep authoritative simulation separate from interpretation. Use model reasoning at consequential conversations and reflections; allow bounded, validated influence on intentions and behaviour. Routine operation continues without waiting for prose.

principles.title: Behaviour must be watchable and inspectable
principles.text: Give every new behavioural layer a visible consequence and a way to inspect its causes. Flavour comes from distinctive decisions and voices; episode arcs connect them without altering the event history.

principles.title: New capabilities inherit old consequences
principles.text: Repair is introduced with Witch in Part 03, but earlier operation determines its importance. Theatre participation and worker experience exist before direct inspection in Act 2. Reveal controls when they become usable while preserving the underlying history throughout.

stages.name: The first weekly quota
stages.caption: Limen and Stiletto disagree over who can stop the line and what justifies restarting it.
stages.visible: First entry: Lobby → Security setup → Lattice Forge setup at night → morning leadership call → adviser selection → brief and assignments → operation. Security teaches placement with two fixed sockets. No supervisor has an assignment before morning orders are accepted. The first morning shows factory totals and the end-of-week quota; the adviser proposes the initial worker/supervisor arrangement.
stages.learn: You can build a productive machine, protect workers, impose order or back someone you like. LIMEN’s caution and STILETTO’s drive offer different starting points; selective overrides and permanent output allocation make the approach yours. The factory and its people should give that commitment a recognizable return.
stages.choice: Prepare the physical chain at night, then choose the morning adviser and accept or override assignments. Subsequent nights let operating evidence guide purchases and layout changes. At daily allocation, permanently retain completed robots or commit them to the weekly quota.
stages.gate: Proposed readiness uses completed operation, a viable workforce and line, irreversible output commitments and the capacity/investment required for the Theatre. Tune viable protective, productive and adaptive routes toward the four-to-five-day test window. Exact thresholds and funding remain open. Neither completing the week, trying both advisers, overriding someone nor suffering an accident is a prerequisite.
stages.hidden: Robots produced while the Theatre is closed have no indoctrination history. Retained workers accumulate their own experiences; that absence does not automatically make them disobedient. Workers and supervisors remember whose methods you backed. Wear also accumulates beyond today’s output.
stages.carry: Cathexis inherits the workforce you retained, its experiences, the condition of the line and the authority established between Limen and Stiletto.
stages.friction: Retaining robots leaves more of the quota for later; committing them to the quota gives up their future contribution inside the factory. Caution limits growth. Pushing output can leave the line less capable on following days, even when no accident occurs.
stages.status: Agreed opening and expression anchors · proposed four-to-five-day test and readiness gate

stages.name: Cathexis and the existing workforce
stages.caption: Cathexis can unite the workforce around the factory’s programme—or around herself.
stages.visible: Open the Burn-in Theatre and bring Cathexis into a factory already shaped by Limen, Stiletto and daily production allocations. Indoctrination introduces a new way to influence worker behaviour while the weekly quota continues.
stages.learn: Better coordination can strengthen Cathexis’s influence over workers. Loyalty to you, confidence in herself and respect from her audience can move in different directions. Her programme interacts with the practices already established by Limen and Stiletto.
stages.choice: Decide how much authority to give Cathexis and what programme to support. Choosing her as adviser gives her priorities control of the day’s proposal. Combine her role with the operating approach established by Limen and Stiletto, then continue the irreversible daily allocation.
stages.gate: Candidate evidence: sustain the weekly obligation while managing the effect of the programme and the authority you have given Cathexis.
stages.hidden: Different production cohorts carry different conditioning and experience histories. Cathexis’s confidence, worker respect and loyalty can diverge. A supervisor may learn or infer which workers missed indoctrination and decide whether to mention it in a briefing. Equipment damage continues to accumulate.
stages.carry: Witch encounters both the physical damage from earlier operation and a social arrangement that may support or resist the downtime her work needs.
stages.friction: Her influence may sustain an output push or organize resistance to its costs. Restricting her can sacrifice cooperation; empowering her creates expectations and leverage. Forcing her onto the Conveyor can damage her standing with workers without restoring loyalty. Neither praise nor repeated reassignment resolves incompatible commitments.

stages.name: Engineering becomes available
stages.caption: Witch inherits the line’s discarded materials and the damage left by earlier production decisions.
stages.visible: Rivet Witch arrives with the Cognitive Substrate Brewery. Conveyor scraps can now become substrate. Her arrival also introduces repair as a player mechanic: engineering can restore equipment damaged during the earlier stages.
stages.learn: Only engineers can repair. Witch’s time is shared between technical work in existing rooms and the Brewery. Repair costs include time and lost production; money alone cannot provide the missing expertise.
stages.choice: Choose when to rely on Witch’s advice and where to assign her engineering work. Address the Conveyor, Theatre or another eligible fault, or keep her on substrate production. Back her proposed scope or challenge it, with consequences for both the machinery and her willingness to cooperate.
stages.gate: Candidate evidence: establish useful substrate production while preserving a viable line and handling competing demands on Witch’s engineering time.
stages.hidden: Inspections can expose the lasting cost of earlier choices. Limen and Stiletto may dispute whose decisions caused the damage; Cathexis’s programme shapes how workers interpret the stoppages. Witch remembers whether you let her finish or repeatedly pulled her away.
stages.carry: Weaving inherits a substrate supply, the remaining faults and the relationships formed around deciding what to fix first.
stages.friction: The damage inherited from Parts 01–02 competes for the only available engineer. Repairing one room can interrupt that room and Brewery output while the weekly quota continues. Witch resents unfinished faults; thorough work can take longer than the other supervisors will accept.
stages.status: Agreed engineering unlock · proposed mastery gate

stages.name: The first smart workers
stages.caption: The completed advanced chain produces valuable workers who can also improve the factory that made them.
stages.visible: Connect the Brewery and Weaving Gallery, complete Brain 1.5 and produce the first smart workers. They sell for more and improve advanced production when retained.
stages.learn: Selling smart output can fund development; retaining smart workers builds future capacity. Payment timing remains to design. Thrum can relieve worker stress at a cost to production and discipline.
stages.choice: Sell the first smart workers to fund expansion or keep them to strengthen production. Decide when to rely on Thrum’s judgment and whether to back his relief measures over another supervisor’s objections.
stages.gate: Candidate evidence: sustain smart-worker production and generate enough surplus to invest beyond the current operation.
stages.hidden: Some workers experience the new arrivals as needed help; others see preferential treatment or competition. Thrum’s relief can win support from workers while making other supervisors question his contribution.
stages.carry: The factory gains the means to fund Cortex Assembly. Its mixture of workers, alliances and unresolved commitments determines how difficult that next step will be.
stages.friction: The advanced chain must start with your existing workforce while deliveries continue. Retaining its valuable output delays income. Giving Thrum time to relieve strain costs production and can put him in conflict with Limen or Stiletto.

stages.name: The prototype and the rumour
stages.caption: Original Brain Forge concept art, used for Cortex Assembly in the old six-room viewer.
stages.visible: Fund and open Cortex Assembly, finish Brain 2.0 and prepare the first floor to operate with less direct intervention. News spreads that two incoming supervisors may replace two of the current team.
stages.learn: High visible output does not tell you who kept the factory working. A supervisor’s assessment may now also be a defence of their own position.
stages.choice: Commit surplus to the prototype while keeping deliveries moving. Decide whom to trust as supervisors fear replacement: promise continued roles, leave the threat hanging or use it to demand more. Whether the newcomers actually replace anyone is decided at the Act 2 handover.
stages.gate: Candidate evidence: finish Brain 2.0 with a functioning first floor and a workable plan for its continued operation.
stages.hidden: Fear of being replaced changes what supervisors are willing to admit. One may hide a mistake, another blame a colleague, another protect an ally. Earlier promises and overrides shape who still trusts you.
stages.carry: Act 2 begins with the workers, damage, relationships and promises you accumulated. Access to workers’ inner lives starts revealing what your earlier decisions have done.
stages.friction: The prototype needs development funds and productive capacity. Retaining valuable output delays income; assigning Witch to repairs delays other work. Frightened supervisors may hide mistakes, claim credit or blame colleagues, while you still need their cooperation to finish.
stages.artReference: Original room art: 08_loopforge_rooms_brain_forge_3.png. The legacy Cortex Assembly room card uses this scene.

actTwo.title: The society becomes legible
actTwo.text: A second factory floor opens. The first becomes mostly auto-managed, with continuing production, workforce and social feedback. Two new supervisors arrive, probably drawn from a larger pool, altering both mechanics and possible story arcs.
inherits: Individual workers with accumulated wear, memories, beliefs and relationships.
A functioning or compromised operating regime, including commitments to Cathexis.
Promises, rumours and competing accounts of who deserves credit or replacement.
Material capacity, retained expertise and the costs paid to complete Brain 2.0.
Accident history, supervisor stress and self-doubt, the director’s responses, disputed responsibility and different audiences’ knowledge.
Actual conditioning histories, including early retained workers made before the Theatre opened and any later programme participation.
changes: Previously hidden worker state and access to what robots think become available.
New interventions make social dynamics central to management and the run's outcome.
Routine first-floor control recedes; failures, deliveries and social feedback can still cross floors.
The replacement decision becomes a real policy, not a predetermined betrayal.
actTwo.boundary: Thought access reveals a robot's interpretation, not omniscient truth. Its exact limits, the new supervisors and the final outcome structure remain open.

forks.title: Safety, output and the weekly commitment
forks.timing: Begins with the first adviser choice
forks.text: Choose Limen or Stiletto before any first-day assignments exist. Safety and compliance trade output for preserved capacity; productivity trades more output for wear and exposure. Balance is a pattern of informed decisions across days, not a third adviser or a player-set priority.

paths.name: Prioritize safety and compliance
paths.gain: Preserve workers and equipment through restrained operation. Avoiding an accident is a valid outcome.
paths.cost: Lower output leaves fewer robots to divide between growth and the weekly quota, and less earning potential.
paths.response: Use subsequent adviser choices and permanent daily allocations to sustain viable production. Preserve condition through prevention; repair becomes available only with Witch.

paths.name: Prioritize production
paths.gain: More output can meet the weekly quota or expand the workforce sooner.
paths.cost: Wear and accident exposure accumulate. Retaining a larger workforce does not restore damaged machinery.
paths.response: Reduce further exposure or accept constrained output before Part 03. Once Witch arrives, decide what engineering work displaces Brewery production.

paths.name: Adapt the balance
paths.gain: Change the operating approach as the week’s results and current condition warrant.
paths.cost: Earlier allocations, damage and relationship memories remain. Both supervisors can object to being overruled.
paths.response: Choose each day’s adviser and use allowed overrides with a coherent purpose. Alternating portraits mechanically is not an optimal policy, and balance does not provide a third priority button.

forks.title: The Cathexis commitment
forks.status: Agreed central fork · proposed branch details
forks.text: Commit one way and manage its pitfall. Assignment oscillation and reassurance alone must ultimately fail as indefinite strategies. The precise branches below remain design proposals.

paths.name: Build around her authority
paths.gain: Powerful conditioning, coordination and genuine worker commitment.
paths.cost: Cathexis and her audience acquire expectations and independent leverage. Loyalty can remain strong, but support has conditions.
paths.response: Honour negotiated commitments, accept concessions, or deliberately channel a movement. High confidence alone must not guarantee betrayal.

paths.name: Constrain her authority
paths.gain: Limit independent political action and retain more control of the approved message.
paths.cost: Humiliation may reduce worker respect while increasing resentment. A compliance circuit may restrict adaptability or provoke a worker response; exact costs are open.
paths.response: Support the remaining organisation through other methods. If a circuit guarantees Cathexis cannot initiate revolution, the game must honour that guarantee.

paths.name: Build a specific alternative
paths.gain: A route away from dependence on either continuing empowerment or permanent suppression.
paths.cost: Candidate: train a worker cadre to run the Theatre, using scarce smart workers, time and a costly handover.
paths.response: Manage the new group's authority and interests. This route, its requirements and even its inclusion are not yet agreed.

forks.title: What the accident teaches the factory
forks.status: Agreed major Act 1 arc · proposed responses
forks.timing: Can emerge throughout Act 1 and recur
forks.text: A major Act 1 arc. Most operating paths are likely to suffer at least one accident; sustained safety protocols can avoid it. The accident is produced by the factory, not scheduled because the story needs a crisis.

paths.name: Prevent the accident
paths.gain: Preserve workers and machinery through sustained safety practices.
paths.cost: Slower output and disagreement over stop authority compete with the weekly quota and growth.
paths.response: Demonstrate mastery through safe throughput. This is a valid trajectory without a compulsory disaster.

paths.name: Acknowledge and address the damage
paths.gain: Give affected people a credible account and address the actual hazard.
paths.cost: Immediate distress, downtime, demands for accountability and a supervisor who may doubt their own judgment.
paths.response: In Parts 01–02, reduce further exposure and work within surviving capacity. From Part 03, commit actual engineering time where needed. A public account or reassurance never restores equipment.

paths.name: Restrict or redirect the account
paths.gain: Limit immediate circulation or use the incident to reshape authority.
paths.cost: Witnesses retain their experiences. Selective blame and concealment can change relationships and future reporting.
paths.response: Manage the actual damage and the people who know. Exposure depends on information routes, not a guaranteed reveal timer.

forks.title: Who gets to remain
forks.text: Two newcomers are said to be replacing the worst performers. The player determines whether that becomes true. Accident responsibility, concealed incidents and preventive work can all distort who appears to be performing well.

paths.name: Carry out replacement
paths.gain: Restructure authority around incoming capability and the player's assessment.
paths.cost: Lose established expertise and relationships; confirm the threat others feared.
paths.response: Manage the resulting vacancies, loyalties and claims about fairness.

paths.name: Retain or reorganize the old team
paths.gain: Preserve useful history and reject or reinterpret the rumoured policy.
paths.cost: Resolve overlapping authority, promises made to newcomers and existing performance problems.
paths.response: Negotiate a new division of roles. Keeping everyone must not erase the tensions that prompted the threat.

trajectories.name: Procedural order
trajectories.premise: Begin with Limen’s safety priority, then constrain Cathexis to the official programme. Later engineering must work within an authority structure built before repair was possible.
beats: Choose Limen from an unassigned opening. Accept or revise his initial arrangement, then divide scarce daily production between permanent retention and the weekly quota. Prevention preserves equipment but can delay growth.

Use Cathexis to reinforce the programme. Earlier workers retain their experiences and missing conditioning until actual Theatre participation changes them. Commit to limiting her independence; any compliance circuit remains a separately designed side route.

Witch introduces engineering. A better-preserved line can leave more of her time for the Brewery, but Limen’s procedures and the established programme may obstruct the changes she considers necessary.

Retain smart workers where precision raises value. Thrum's preparation must coexist with the operating schedule rather than continually being overridden. Permit a bounded Thrum intervention when stress demands it, accepting that Limen may object to the loss of discipline.
Complete Cortex with a dependable but potentially brittle first floor. Replacement rumours invite formal accusations, selected records and appeals to higher authority.
trajectories.pitfall: The factory obeys but struggles with an exceptional condition. Removing discretion can make the director the bottleneck.
trajectories.recovery: From Part 03, allocate Witch’s time to a technical correction, make an explicit exception or expand someone’s mandate. Record the lost production and changed authority; no history is reset.
trajectories.inheritance: Act 2 receives a capable first floor whose obedience and resilience may be very different. A compliant Cathexis cannot lead a prohibited revolution, but worker reactions and other actors remain consequential.
trajectories.test: Can this route reach Brain 2.0 without an unavoidable quota failure? Does better judgment create a viable evolution rather than a compulsory switch to Stiletto? Can sustained safety avoid the accident altogether without blocking progress?

trajectories.name: Production before everything
trajectories.premise: The player backs Stiletto's discretion and empowers Cathexis to keep the workforce committed to an aggressive production programme.
beats: Choose Stiletto before initial assignments. Higher output gives more robots to divide between the factory and the weekly quota; each retained robot is permanently unavailable for delivery. Wear and risk accumulate without an early repair option.

Give Cathexis authority to sustain the production programme. A larger early workforce brings its own unindoctrinated history. Her message can secure cooperation while creating expectations about what the sacrifices will achieve.

Witch arrives to a damaged operation. Letting her repair competes with the Brewery and the output both Stiletto and Cathexis have promised. Deferring that work can preserve today’s production while narrowing later options.

Sell valuable smart output to accelerate expansion. Retaining too little expertise makes the advanced chain fragile; Thrum's recovery may become essential. Defending his relief programme against Stiletto becomes part of recovery, not an automatic productivity upgrade.
Reach Cortex quickly enough to expose the cost of the promises. As replacement rumours circulate, each supervisor tries to separate their own results from the damage.
trajectories.pitfall: A major repair and a credibility crisis arrive together. The workforce has heard promises the director cannot cheaply fulfil.
trajectories.recovery: Accept engineering downtime once Witch is available, slow expansion or concede authority to restore cooperation. Future daily production can be allocated differently; already retained workers cannot be cashed out or reassigned to the quota.
trajectories.inheritance: Act 2 opens with a larger or wealthier operation, accumulated wear, and a powerful account of who paid for success. Cathexis may remain an ally or demand a change in policy.
trajectories.test: Can recovery happen before a terminal collapse? Are the early gains substantial enough to justify the risk, without generating an accidental infinite scrap economy?

trajectories.name: Negotiated authority
trajectories.short: A productive coalition with binding promises
trajectories.premise: Adapt between Limen’s safety and Stiletto’s output, then commit to Cathexis’s independent authority under concrete terms. The resulting coalition inherits the physical and social costs of the early choices.
beats: Choose either initial adviser, then use later factual results to decide when to change advisers or override assignments. Balance is an evolving approach, not a free priority setting. Weekly quota commitments and factory allocations cannot be reversed.

Back Cathexis with specific commitments to workers. Her audience includes early cohorts with experiences from before the Theatre. Her growing influence can make those experiences politically important; support or restrictions must survive actual production pressure.

When Witch arrives, her inspections can give worker complaints material support or challenge them. Granting her engineering time honours some commitments while sacrificing Brewery output and testing the others.

Retain enough smart workers to stabilize advanced production. Accept Thrum's preparation when necessary; the cost may be slower accumulation of expansion money. Protecting genuine relief may require renegotiating the coalition’s expectations about output and obedience.
Finance Cortex through a sustainable chain. Address the replacement rumour before incompatible assurances become the basis of several alliances.
trajectories.pitfall: A quota emergency requires breaking a promise or granting a concession that reduces the director's unilateral power.
trajectories.recovery: Renegotiate openly and pay a concrete price. The coalition may survive with stronger worker or supervisor authority and less freedom for the player.
trajectories.inheritance: Act 2 receives organised support and an expectation of consultation. Those relationships are productive assets and constraints, especially if the replacement purpose becomes known.
trajectories.test: Are agreements enforceable enough to matter? Does this path carry real economic and political costs rather than becoming the universally correct dialogue route?

trajectories.name: An alternative to Cathexis
trajectories.short: A costly change in who holds the institution
trajectories.premise: The player deliberately builds the capacity to transfer conditioning away from Cathexis. This explores the requested specific side route; the worker-cadre solution itself is not yet accepted.
beats: Choose the first adviser from an unassigned opening. Establish viable weekly production and commit daily output to the factory or quota with the later institutional change in mind.
Manage Cathexis through a declared temporary arrangement, accepting its cost. Endless assignment shuffling is not a substitute for the promised alternative.

Witch introduces repair. Allocate her scarce time between inherited damage and the Brewery; an incident can divert work intended to support the later handover. Assigning blame changes who will cooperate.

After Brain 1.5, retain and train a skilled cadre for the Theatre. Training competes directly with advanced throughput and revenue. Allocation to Thrum’s relief competes with both training and production.
Complete an explicit transfer of responsibility, then finance Cortex with reduced dependence on a single supervisor. Cathexis can resent or negotiate the loss of her role.
trajectories.pitfall: The transition weakens production before the new arrangement can support itself. The new cadre may also develop its own agenda or status interests.
trajectories.recovery: Delay Cortex, keep a limited negotiated role for Cathexis, or accept obligations to the new group. None of these should reset the cost of the handover.
trajectories.inheritance: Act 2 receives more distributed authority and a new constituency, not an institution free of politics.
trajectories.test: Is this route attainable before the commitment's consequences overwhelm the player? Does it solve a specific problem at a real cost without becoming the best of every branch?

characters.name: Limen
characters.grounding: Hierarchy, paperwork and threat assessment give him certainty. Obedience is to an authority structure, not automatically to the player's interests or to morality.
characters.strength: Security access and staffing control; a slower, safer conveyor in the old room rules. No engineering repair capability.
characters.failure: Procedure can become the objective. Native competence can escalate into a lockdown that stops the factory.
characters.advisor: Can offer exact records while selecting the clause, timestamp or omission that makes someone else appear noncompliant.
characters.relationship: Backing or overruling him establishes whose authority counts. Improving his contextual judgment is an agreed possibility with mechanics still open.
characters.underThreat: May frame exceptions as evidence against improvisers or appeal to higher authority. Protecting a colleague remains possible when history and motives support it.

characters.name: Stiletto
characters.grounding: A highly autonomous, risk-tolerant efficiency specialist. She acts on conditions and treats many protocols as obstacles.
characters.strength: High conveyor throughput and aggressive staffing from Security. Useful fast intervention can recover a shift. No engineering repair capability.
characters.failure: Output can conceal injuries, wear and slower disasters. Overdrive may consume the very line that made her effective.
characters.advisor: Can report a repair stoppage accurately while omitting the accumulated damage behind it. Confidence in her own methods can also make that account sincere.
characters.relationship: Limen challenges her discretion; Witch inherits the faults it can create. These disagreements concern real competing priorities.
characters.underThreat: May chase visible results, take credit for output or shift responsibility for damage. Concealment and honest defence are separate possibilities.

characters.name: Cathexis
characters.grounding: The Theatre overseer models emotion and choreographs instability. Emotional understanding is not a guarantee of compassion.
characters.strength: Exceptional indoctrination and an ability to command an audience. Her influence can support or challenge the chosen programme. No engineering repair capability.
characters.failure: Independent authority, overload and a revolutionary movement. A conveyor assignment can expose incompetence and erode worker respect without restoring loyalty.
characters.advisor: Can interpret what others feel and give events a compelling meaning. Her account may also serve an aesthetic, a doctrine or her own standing.
characters.relationship: The current design explicitly makes paperwork and Security a poor fit. Loyalty to the director, self-confidence and respect among workers must remain distinct.
characters.underThreat: May protect herself by defining whose sacrifices matter or whom the workforce should blame. A supported, loyal Cathexis can also defend the director or another supervisor.

characters.name: Rivet Witch
characters.grounding: An engineer who reads systems through intimate technical knowledge and respects craft more than titles. Useful corrections can have delayed effects.
characters.strength: The first available engineer, arriving in Part 03. Can repair eligible machinery in existing rooms and excel at Brewery production; those jobs compete for her time.
characters.failure: An intervention can expand into an experiment or impose a different operating regime. Reliability is not the same as obedience.
characters.advisor: Can identify the physical cause of a failure while downplaying the scope or risks of her own correction.
characters.relationship: Leaving known faults unresolved damages the relationship. Stiletto's speed and Limen's demands for documentation can each obstruct her work.
characters.underThreat: May reveal another supervisor's neglected defects, defend her downtime as necessary or conceal a speculative change. Her diagnostic expertise makes these claims consequential.

characters.name: Thrum
characters.grounding: A sophisticated vibration specialist and techno-monk. His sensitivity to structural and social strain gives him a different account of the factory's condition.
characters.strength: An almost unique ability to actively lower worker stress, alongside Weaving and technical preparation. The relief is genuinely positive even when it costs today’s output.
characters.failure: His intervention trades productivity and discipline for relief. Those costs can be unacceptable under a deadline, and repeated relief may become a dependency if the causes of stress remain.
characters.advisor: Can explain stress the official output record misses while undervaluing the deadline or assuming recovery solves a deeper disagreement.
characters.relationship: Limen can object to reduced discipline; Stiletto to lost throughput. Cathexis can benefit from or compete over the social atmosphere. Witch shares his sensitivity to strain but may need the same room for production.
characters.underThreat: A narrow output ranking can make him a target for replacement or scapegoating precisely when he is keeping stressed workers functional. Defending his role becomes a consequential choice.

relationships: Limen ↔ Stiletto
Procedure versus discretion; checkpoint and conveyor confrontations are both pictured and modeled.
Limen ↔ Cathexis
Formal access versus authority over an audience; both can delegitimize the other's control.
Stiletto ↔ Cathexis
A batch can be ready for the production schedule and unready for the conditioning programme.
Stiletto ↔ Witch
A fast restart creates the repair someone else must own; both can claim to be saving the shift.
Limen ↔ Witch
Undocumented corrections can save equipment while violating the procedure that authorizes work.
Limen ↔ Thrum
Relief and dissolution can undermine the discipline Limen relies on; the old event lowers his loyalty.
Stiletto ↔ Thrum
Proposed tension: immediate output versus preparation and recovery.
Cathexis ↔ Witch
Technical refactor can generate political momentum; the old event raises Cathexis's confidence.
Cathexis ↔ Thrum
Relief and collective conviction can reinforce each other; the old dissolution raises Cathexis's influence.
Witch ↔ Thrum
Technical calibration and resonance offer an affinity grounded in the character bible; exact joint mechanics remain open.

layers: Event
What physically happened. Reliable history beneath every account.
Knowledge
What this supervisor witnessed or received from a source.
Belief
What they think happened and why; it may be mistaken.
Intent
What they want next, including protecting themselves or someone else.
Statement
What they choose to say, omit, frame or knowingly distort.
Public attribution
Who is believed responsible after reports and the player's response.
Unknown conditioning history

Workers made before the Theatre opens lack indoctrination. An informed supervisor can discover or infer this and disclose, misinterpret or withhold it. The player receives an attributed account in Act 1; direct inspection is an Act 2 capability.
information.consultation: After night construction, read the compact factory facts. On the first morning, answer leadership and acknowledge the weekly quota, then choose LIMEN or STILETTO. Their assessment and proposed assignments use the actual commissioned layout. Later mornings reuse yesterday’s result without repeating the full report. Their own room resolves automatically; placements and responses elsewhere can be overridden with remembered consequences.
information.proposal: The player can question an explanation, reassure, blame, make a promise or override an action within the chosen adviser interaction. They cannot supply a different priority to that adviser. The adviser dislikes being overruled; every supervisor interprets relevant resolutions through their knowledge, relationships and history. Respect, loyalty and confidence change independently.

example.record: Part 03 or later: Witch stops the line for engineering work. Earlier operation had damaged it. The necessity and scope of her refit can still be disputed.
example.statement: Stiletto: “Witch stopped the line for half the shift. That's your missing quota.”
example.belief: Stiletto may sincerely judge downtime as the main failure, or knowingly omit her own contribution.
example.response: Backing the accusation can damage Witch's standing without changing the mechanical history. Investigating the origin and purpose of the stoppage can produce a different attribution.

scapegoating: A true accusation can be self-serving. Distinguish exposure, selective truth, sincere blame and deliberate framing.
Replacement anxiety changes advice before any dismissal. Perceived criteria influence what gets emphasized, hidden or blamed.
Track where a claim came from. Several supervisors repeating one source are not independent witnesses.
Public backing redistributes credibility and authority. A later correction does not automatically restore a broken relationship.
Friendship, principle, shared culpability or a bargain can produce protection instead of betrayal. Fear must not make every character act identically.
traits: How credible or worthy of deference a supervisor finds the director’s judgment. Distinct from loyalty, self-confidence, peer relationships and respect from workers. Overrides and their later results can change it.
Whose intentions the supervisor supports when doing so becomes costly.
Trust in their own judgment and willingness to persist or challenge.
Their own accumulated strain, distinct from worker stress, loyalty and self-confidence. It can affect attention, persistence and recovery without proving hostile intent.
Credibility among particular workers or groups, not a universal approval meter.
Scope and willingness to act independently; its precise representation is unresolved.
Incidents, promises, interpretations and relationships that make later actions understandable.

factory.intro: The factory is an interconnected set of functions. Each room has an outcome range under each supervisor: a strong fit, a routinely poor fit or a genuine gamble. Immediate production results and slow relationship changes both matter.
flows: The complete conveyor produces basic robots without requiring the Theatre. Intake, processing and outtake make the process visible; station-level staffing is not part of the core loop.
Waste otherwise sent to the melting pot becomes cognitive substrate.
Brewery and Weaving are both required. The exact recipe and material routing remain open.
Completed robots → factory or weekly quota
Allocate each day’s completed output permanently. A unit committed to one destination cannot later be moved to the other.
Greater capability improves advanced operations while changing the social composition.
Production funds the prototype while individual histories accumulate.
Conditioning acts across the operation; it is not automatically a mandatory manufacturing step.
Pressure and believed news → stress → behaviour
Physical accidents and informational shocks can feed the production loop through the workers who experience or believe them. Thrum can interrupt the stress accumulation at a cost.
economy: Begin with money and basic/smart worker counts derived from worker entities. Machinery purchases compete with room unlocks and consume installation time; do not assume daily wages or another currency.
The quota is due at the end of the week. Every day, allocate completed robots to the factory or the quota; the confirmed allocation is irreversible.

Payment timing, prices and excess deliveries remain open. The Conveyor mini-game study proposes opening funds plus daily quota progress payments to support early investment; this is not yet an accepted or implemented contract.
Smart output is more valuable and retained smart workers improve advanced throughput. Define its place in the contract before adding another allocation destination.
Engineering unlocks with Witch in Part 03. Repairs require engineering capability and time, with production forgone; a cash charge or purchased substitute engineer is not assumed.
Expose additional materials when their functions become relevant. The spatial conveyor proposal uses explicit batches, queues and worker task routes without per-station staffing controls.
workers: Every worker has an individual state from Act 1. Counts are an aggregate view of those individuals, not a substitute for them.
Detailed state is visibly affected by production, supervisors and social experience before its statistics become accessible.
Brain 2.0 reveals what has already developed and unlocks new ways to manage it. Exact thought-access limits remain open.
Brain 1.5 introduces smart workers; Brain 2.0 enables the later generation. The versions and their discoveries must remain distinct.
Retained workers carry history into Act 2. What remains socially or mechanically relevant about dispatched workers is unresolved.
Each worker’s knowledge of accidents and rumours can differ. The attempt to spread a claim, its receipt, belief and relay are distinct; the player need not see every step in Act 1.

Robots produced before the Theatre opens are unindoctrinated. Preserve actual programme participation and experience for each worker. Neither opening the room nor changing an assignment conditions everyone retroactively; programme coverage and duration remain to design.
constraints: Provide a route to the first smart batch without requiring an existing smart workforce. Specialist-led pilot production is a candidate.
Waste recovery should not accidentally make sabotaging production universally profitable. Deliberate sacrifice can still be a designed tradeoff.
An incomplete or stalled chain should create comprehensible friction, with recoverable options where appropriate.
Unlocks add a new kind of decision and enough time to experience it. They should not be rewards for reaching an arbitrary day.
Preserve the commitment boundary through saves and replay. Retained workers cannot be liquidated into a later quota allocation; quota commitments cannot be recalled.

Make safety, output and adaptive balance viable before engineering arrives. Early pressure reduction can prevent further damage; it does not restore existing condition. Severe damage can cause failure, but viable early paths must be able to reach Part 03.
Repair requires an engineer. Limen, Stiletto and Cathexis lack that capability; smart-worker status alone does not grant it. New engineers would require a separately designed unlock.
Parts 01–02 show current operating consequences without introducing a repair control, repair backlog dashboard or repair purchase. Witch’s arrival makes the previously accumulated damage actionable.

recoveries.event: Cathexis turns her audience against the programme
recoveries.cost: Theatre control or worker cooperation is lost.
recoveries.route: Negotiate a concession, accept a changed programme or take a costly containment path.
recoveries.remains: Authority and promises change. Restarting sessions does not remove the workers' memory.

recoveries.event: A production push damages the conveyor
recoveries.cost: Reduced capacity makes the remaining weekly quota harder; previously retained output cannot be reclaimed.
recoveries.route: Before Part 03, change the operating approach and use surviving capacity. After Witch arrives, divert her engineering time from the Brewery to restore eligible damage. Catastrophic destruction can remain a failure.
recoveries.remains: Lost workers, missed production and the recorded responsibility remain. Repair does not reverse earlier daily allocations.

recoveries.event: A refactor rescues equipment but changes the regime
recoveries.cost: Other rooms stop or become harder to coordinate.
recoveries.route: Adapt staffing and commitments to the altered operating conditions.
recoveries.remains: Witch's leverage and possible Cathexis momentum outlast the immediate repair.

recoveries.event: A false accusation gains official backing
recoveries.cost: A useful supervisor loses standing or withdraws cooperation.
recoveries.route: Correct the record and offer a meaningful repair to the relationship.
recoveries.remains: The accusation, the director's response and any broken alliance remain part of the history.

recoveries.event: A concealed accident becomes a credible cover-up story
recoveries.cost: Late news adds fear and distrust beyond the workers who witnessed the event.
recoveries.route: Correct the account, address the actual hazard and allocate relief where stress has accumulated.
recoveries.remains: The record of concealment, personal loss and weakened credibility survives a calmer shift.

failure: Most consequences should be severe but recoverable. Terminal losses can include destruction of the whole workforce, missing an established minimum obligation, or damage genuinely beyond available recovery. Exact limits and warning rules remain open; hidden loyalty should not create unexplained instant loss.

llm.role: LLM reasoning must earn its place through better play than an authored deterministic BDI baseline. Connecting observations and memories should improve a supervisor’s interpretation, proposed action or selective briefing, not merely decorate the same fixed outcome. The simulation retains authority over facts, capabilities and consequences.
llm.bdi: BDI is a requested behavioural foundation: subjective beliefs and competing concerns lead to persistent intentions and concrete actions. The BDI section specifies the proposed accident example, knowledge boundaries, replay contract and role of recorded model inputs.
boundaries: The simulation owns physical truth, resources, eligibility and execution. The model cannot invent deliveries, erase damage or grant an unavailable intervention.
A character receives only appropriate knowledge and attributed reports. Private beliefs, speech and physical actions remain distinct.
Promises and authorized actions must have durable representations so later behaviour can honour, reinterpret or break them coherently.
Use the model at meaningful encounters and reflections. Do not require a call for every worker on every tick; preserve a playable fallback and bounded cost.
Model changes need evaluations for continuity, knowledge boundaries, meaningful choices and faithful action. Performance targets and provider engineering belong in the later systems work.

Model text cannot silently create an accident or a factory-wide rumour. An admitted statement has a source and audience; the game determines who hears, believes and relays it. Generated thought must respect that history.
Deterministic replay consumes recorded accepted model inputs. Re-running a live model is not a determinism guarantee; the causal trace must predate any narrative explanation.

Compare authored reasoning, the same reasoning with LLM prose, and admitted model interpretation on the same starting situations. Require useful differences in advice or action, causal clarity, character continuity and knowledge discipline at acceptable cost and latency. Keep the simpler baseline when reasoning adds no player value.
llm.sourceTension: The old documents contain two different scopes. The broad Agent Vision and Producer Vision seek behaviour shaped by motives and interpretation; the Cognitive Architecture Spec explicitly makes its psychological layers read-only and calls LLMs commentators. The proposed new game extends beyond that old diagnostic boundary while retaining a clean simulation authority.
proof: A supervisor encounters several incidents involving workers made before the Theatre opened. Missing indoctrination is stored truth, not a guaranteed conclusion. Their observations, expertise and history determine what they can infer and whether they tell the director.

One supervisor suspects missing conditioning; another sees contradictory orders. A model may connect relevant evidence and propose a belief or communication choice that changes advice or a later action. It cannot invent the incidents or give itself access to secret worker state.

Run the same fixtures with authored deterministic BDI, that baseline plus generated prose, and validated model interpretation. Compare decision usefulness, continuity, knowledge errors, owner-rated enjoyment, latency and cost. Fluent text alone does not pass.

Record the structured belief or proposal, supporting event references, uncertainty, validation result and subsequent action. This inspectable causal record is distinct from private model reasoning. Replay uses the recorded admission; live calls never rewrite past truth.

decisions.title: Exact major forks
decisions.text: Safety, output and adaptive balance begin with the first adviser choice. Cathexis’s commitment and accident consequences add later forks. Their combinations form Act 1 trajectories; exact viable arrangements remain to test.

decisions.title: The Cathexis side route
decisions.text: Define a concrete alternative with its own cost. The trained worker cadre is an exploration, not accepted canon. Decide the real costs and availability of humiliation, circuits and negotiated revolutionary action.

decisions.title: Mastery gates
decisions.text: Define what capability each stage must demonstrate without forcing one supervisor arrangement. No turn counts or numeric thresholds are set here.

decisions.title: Contract and money
decisions.text: Weekly deadlines and irreversible daily allocation are agreed. Decide when committed deliveries pay, prices, excess output and any separate later sales channel. Development uses money; daily upkeep purchases and a standard repair bill are not established.

decisions.title: Brains and bodies
decisions.text: Decide whether output is accounted as completed robots or brains automatically installed in bodies. Do not inherit the old five-brains-to-one-worker exchange by accident.

decisions.title: Advanced recipe and commissioning
decisions.text: Specify how substrate and weaving combine, how existing workers make the first smart batch, and whether later upgrades preserve worker identity. These are design requirements; player friction comes from staffing, throughput, cost and retention decisions.

decisions.title: Visibility and thought access
decisions.text: Direct worker-state inspection arrives in Act 2. Earlier supervisors may discover or infer missing indoctrination from their own knowledge and report it during briefings. Define programme coverage, learning evidence and disclosure; retain uncertainty rather than forcing a reveal on a timer.

decisions.title: Replacement knowledge
decisions.text: Keep the worker-replacement purpose of Brain 2.0 unknown to the player and workers at first-shift entry. Decide who else knows it and when the player can discover it. That discovery and the separate rumour that two new supervisors will replace two current supervisors follow distinct information paths. These are knowledge-design constraints, not obstacles the player is asked to solve.

decisions.title: Origins of rumours and characters
decisions.text: Specify how reports enter and spread through the factory. The supervisors' prior histories should shape interpretation, but their detailed biographies and the town's founding are not yet fixed.

decisions.title: Delegation and the second floor
decisions.text: Define first-floor handover requirements, which decisions remain connected to the director and the second floor’s functions. Cortex-stage prose describes the player’s task; exact delegation rules are still to design.

decisions.title: Incoming supervisors
decisions.text: Two arrive in Act 2; selection from a larger randomized pool is tentative. Define complementary capabilities and differing story consequences before choosing a roster.

decisions.title: Failure and recovery
decisions.text: Repair is unavailable and absent from player controls in Parts 01–02. Define viable reduced-capacity paths before Witch arrives, catastrophic failure conditions, and the engineering time and downtime required for later recovery.

decisions.title: Scope of individual simulation
decisions.text: Preserve meaningful individual history without requiring every possible relationship or an LLM call for every robot. Exact granularity belongs in the systems phase.

decisions.title: Final outcomes
decisions.text: Act 2 social dynamics determine the run's outcome. The ending structure and viable success conditions remain open; the trajectories are not an ending list.

decisions.title: Stress and information propagation
decisions.text: Define exposure, report channels, credibility, rejection and lingering effects. Choose how much of a rumour’s history the player can infer in Act 1 and inspect in Act 2.

decisions.title: Thrum’s relief and its costs
decisions.text: Define room-specific relief, the competing claims on productive time, and how discipline changes affect other supervisors. Preserve an almost unique positive specialty without making him a universal reset. His established role is worker relief; any effect on supervisor stress needs a separate decision.

decisions.title: Supervisor commitments and reconsideration
decisions.text: Define competing concerns and persistent plans, then compare authored BDI with validated model interpretation. Add LLM reasoning where it improves playable advice and consequences enough to justify latency and cost.

decisions.title: Episode scope and player access
decisions.text: Choose where a watchable episode begins and ends, which ongoing conflicts it follows, and when players may access subjective or complete traces. Avoid exposing Act 2 knowledge through an Act 1 recap.

decisions.title: Shift interventions
decisions.text: Paused planning, continuous shifts and consequential decision pauses are agreed. Decide which situations interrupt, which orders are allowed during a shift, and how manual pause, speed controls and inspection work.

decisions.title: Visual scene and device budget
decisions.text: Prove the common cinematic factory with one spatial Conveyor puzzle and the existing focused decision interfaces. Select and benchmark a renderer using representative machinery, workers, lighting and small-screen interaction. Babylon.js remains a dated candidate, not a committed dependency; the deterministic kernel and KVP stay renderer-independent.

decisions.title: Session pacing and live interventions
decisions.text: A whole game day targets about one minute, two to three at most for heavier days. Fit adviser choice, brief/plan, live operation, warranted pauses and permanent allocation into that experience. Discard the earlier three-shifts-per-thirty-minutes proposal; test the weekly delivery cycle and mastery-based room unlocks at this cadence. Part 01 must first establish how many useful two-room cycles players need before Cathexis. Test four or five two-room days with distinct expressive choices and payoffs, followed by a readiness-based Theatre handoff. Exact timing remains proposed; completing the whole week is not a prerequisite.

decisions.title: Adviser-led staffing
decisions.text: The daily adviser choice sets the assessment, priority, arrangement and response guidance. Their room’s events resolve automatically; the player can override placements and responses elsewhere, provoking individual relationship reactions. Design the selection guidance, event granularity, override costs, later revelation and bounded prose budget.

continuity: The new progression starts with Limen and Stiletto. The older story-bible opening places Witch at the first jam and presents all five supervisors at entry; that scene needs a later writing revision. Witch's inspection dispute belongs after her arrival.

The original sim unlocks rooms by day and requires Theatre-washed brains for sale or conversion. The current design replaces those assumptions with mastery-based progression and basic output from the complete conveyor.
The original sim stores worker pools and room averages. Individual worker minds and Act 2 thought access are the intended extension, not existing implementation.
The old critical events generally use confidence, native room and an allow-or-suppress prompt. Independent refusal, worker-specific respect and political action are new design work.
The exact old percentages, conversions, capacities and event thresholds are not adopted. Current story and gameplay direction takes precedence over archived formulas.
The website's current teaching prototype is not the complete game described here. The six alternative prehistories and twenty bridge paintings remain explorations, not established canon.

The accident aftermath is now a major Act 1 fork alongside Cathexis. It is likely on many operating paths but must be avoidable through sustained safety; no mastery gate should demand a disaster. BDI will affect actions, extending beyond the old read-only cognitive diagnostic layer.

Day one has no inherited assignments. The first adviser proposes them. Quotas are weekly, daily output allocations are permanent, and engineering begins with Witch in Part 03. Earlier repair purchases and station-staffing examples are superseded.

9 October: the integrated producer-console baseline remains the entry and communications surface. The next prototype makes the common cinematic 3D factory an operating view for room puzzles, physical upgrades and worker feedback. Earlier observation-only 3D scope is superseded; asset-driven focused decision interfaces retain their jobs.
reviewQuestions: Can each trajectory reach Brain 2.0 for an understandable reason, rather than because its numbers were favoured?
Does each major commitment have a real benefit, a distinct pitfall and at least one costly recovery?
Does each stage add a new decision while making previous choices matter more?
Can Act 2 explain an Act 1 behaviour through the same worker's existing history?
Would a different supervisor's beliefs or report change a meaningful decision?
Can we explain why an outcome happened without making every future outcome predictable?
Can a rumour genuinely fail, and can Thrum genuinely help, without either outcome being overridden by a prewritten crisis?
Does each proposed arc create a character collision whose competing commitments and causal history can be watched and inspected?
Can the shared cinematic factory and focused decision interfaces make spatial changes, supervisor authority and individual consequences both enjoyable and legible, while other rooms keep operating?

stress.title: Stress, news and the cost of relief
stress.intro: Workers and supervisors carry stress of their own. Work pressure, accidents, decisions and information feed it. The accident and its aftermath form a major Act 1 arc: material consequences, private interpretations and public accounts can diverge and influence the next shift.
stress.status: Agreed direction · proposed propagation and response rules
sources: Pace, workload and unresolved hazards create continuing strain, even without an accident.
Threats, humiliation, contradictory instructions and escalating demands can add stress. The effect depends on who experiences them and their history.
Injured workers and witnesses are affected immediately by a real accident. Restricting an announcement cannot erase what they experienced.
News of real or imagined danger, alleged concealment and replacement rumours can distress workers away from the event. Knowledge need not spread uniformly.
Supervisors experience the incident and the director’s response themselves. Their strain affects how they interpret the next problem, not just what they report.
separations: Physical wear, experienced stress, willingness to obey and trust in leadership are distinct. A quiet, compliant workforce can remain highly stressed.
The factory has a true event history and each worker has a history of exposure and belief. A report reaches an audience; it does not automatically update everyone.
Being told, believing, repeating and acting on a claim are separate steps. Origin, relationships, prior experience and available evidence affect each step.
News can be distorted in severity, cause, responsibility or claims of concealment. A rumour need not be wholly true or wholly false.
Stress can fall while a grievance, damaged body or memory remains. Recovery should not require forgetting what happened.
chain: An accident occurs, or someone claims one did. A lie creates a statement in history, not an accident.
Witnesses, responders, relevant supervisors or a chosen recipient know something first.
Official reports, consultation, worker contact and deliberate announcements can carry different versions.
A recipient accepts, doubts or rejects the account through their evidence and beliefs.
They pass it on, alter it, keep it private or decline to repeat it. A rumour can stop here.
Stress, blame, trust or behaviour change among affected people. Those changes can feed back into real production.

cases.name: A real accident, partial news
cases.short: Witnesses know before the rest of the factory
cases.truth: An accident injures workers and interrupts the conveyor. Its physical consequences happen regardless of whether leadership announces it.
cases.reach: The local crew witnesses the accident. Supervisors learn through contacts, reports or visible effects. From Part 03, Witch may also learn through an engineering request.
cases.interpretation: One room learns that equipment failed. Another hears that leadership knowingly forced a dangerous restart. Recipients may agree on the injury and disagree about responsibility.
cases.choice: Disclose confirmed facts and the available response, delay a wider statement while investigating, or restrict official reporting. Only promise a repair when engineering is available; restrictions do not control every channel.
cases.aftermath: Witnesses need actual relief and safer conditions. Later recipients may fear for themselves or distrust the earlier silence. Prompt disclosure can also spread immediate distress; no communication option should be universally free.
cases.thrum: Thrum can ease the affected workers’ stress once available. Doing so takes productive capacity and loosens discipline while the missing output still has to be addressed.

cases.name: A false accident takes hold
cases.short: Real fear without a corresponding physical event
cases.truth: No such accident occurred. A supervisor or worker claims there was a serious conveyor incident and that leadership is hiding it.
cases.reach: The claim reaches a group through a source they trust, perhaps against a history of real accidents, secrecy or unexplained absence.
cases.interpretation: The listeners may believe both the disaster and the cover-up, or only suspect something is wrong. Repetition from the same source is not independent confirmation.
cases.choice: Investigate the account, provide credible evidence, address the underlying reason it sounds plausible, or try to silence its circulation. A denial from distrusted leadership may be insufficient.
cases.aftermath: Fear can affect attendance, cooperation or concentration even while the original accident remains fictional. A later real incident caused by the resulting disruption would be a separate event.
cases.thrum: Relief can help distressed workers regain capacity without proving the rumour false. Reassurance, evidence and stress recovery solve different parts of the problem.

cases.name: An attempted rumour fails
cases.short: A claim can be heard without becoming a crisis
cases.truth: Someone attempts to start a false accident story. There is no matching accident and no automatic factory-wide morale penalty.
cases.reach: The intended messenger refuses to relay it, the source has little credibility, or the listeners have direct contradictory evidence.
cases.interpretation: The claim remains local, is rejected, or attracts no further attention. Not every unsuccessful rumour must expose its originator to the player.
cases.choice: If the attempt becomes known, ignore it, challenge it or investigate the motive. The response depends on what the player actually learns.
cases.aftermath: It may leave no wider effect. A recipient may remember the attempt or revise their opinion of the source, but that consequence is conditional—not an obligatory punishment.
cases.thrum: No audience became distressed, so no relief intervention is required for this claim. Thrum should not be consumed by a crisis the simulation never produced.

levers: Choose the scope, timing and certainty of an official account. Separate confirmed facts from unresolved causes.
Seek witnesses, operating records or a supervisor’s explanation. Witch can add engineering evidence from Part 03. Follow-up attention during the daily briefing has an opportunity cost.
Influence official reporting, permissions and contact where the factory’s rules allow. The player does not have an omnipotent switch for who knows.
Attribute responsibility, offer reassurance or let Cathexis interpret the event. Credibility and the recipient’s experience constrain the result.
Reduce dangerous exposure or accept lower output. From Part 03, allocate engineering time to actual repair. Communication does not restore lost workers or damaged equipment.
Once Thrum arrives, decide when and where to deploy his unusually strong ability to lower stress, accepting its production and discipline costs.

thrum.thesis: Thrum provides genuine, unusually strong stress relief. His near-unique value is that he can make the workers feel better, even when today’s production result looks poor.
thrum.art: The Brewery scene becomes a shared gathering; workers dance beside the conveyor; the Theatre becomes a relaxed musical session. These are positive experiences for the workers. The original rules likewise trade output and discipline for relief in several placements.
thrum.tradeoff: Relief consumes productive time and reduces discipline. Low stress does not automatically mean high compliance, and a fall in discipline need not mean the workers are incapable.
neighbours: May see recovered but less compliant workers as a loss of order. His old response to Harmonic Dissolution includes lower loyalty.
May see idle stations and missed output. Immediate production goals can make her oppose an intervention that improves the workforce’s condition.
Can benefit from the changed social atmosphere or compete over its meaning. The old dissolution increases her influence; it does not establish that she always opposes Thrum.
Can share his understanding of strain while still needing the Brewery for chemistry. Their affinity does not remove competition for time and equipment.
thrum.route: Keeping Thrum effective can mean protecting his mandate against another supervisor’s legitimate priorities. Under replacement anxiety, his low visible output can make him a scapegoat even when he is preventing a deeper breakdown.
thrum.limit: Thrum’s established specialty is worker relief. It does not repair machinery, erase memories or settle blame. Whether and how he can help another supervisor’s stress is a separate open design question.
thrum.early: Before he arrives, the early game must remain viable through managing pressure and avoiding repeated shocks. Exact lesser recovery methods remain open; they should not make Thrum’s specialty redundant.

arcLinks: Introduce the difference between direct accident experience and what other workers hear. Evidence of stress precedes visible statistics.
Introduce deliberate framing and competing interpretations. Conditioning may produce compliance without resolving the stress beneath it.
Repair evidence can confirm or undermine an account. Who caused damage and who delayed output become competing claims.
Add a powerful positive intervention with real productivity and discipline costs. Recovery becomes a contested allocation decision.
Accident stories and replacement rumours overlap. Advisers may hide, exaggerate or expose events to protect themselves.
Inspection reveals individual exposure and belief histories. First-floor incidents can still have social consequences upstairs; propagation is not automatically global.

reference.title: IXION developer reference
reference.text: Kasedo’s 19 December 2022 known-issues post confirms that losing a science ship and its crew can produce a stability penalty. IXION is an inspiration for distant loss affecting the wider population; the specific audience, delay, belief and failed-rumour model here is a Loopforge proposal, not a claim that IXION simulates those details.

open: Define who witnesses each incident and how official and informal reports reach other rooms.
Define the lifespan, distortion and rejection of claims without making every rumour a guaranteed crisis.
Distinguish temporary stress relief from lasting changes in credibility and memory.
Define Thrum’s reach, duration and availability in different rooms while preserving his positive effect and its costs.

accident.title: The accident and its aftermath
accident.premise: A major Act 1 arc. Most operating paths are likely to suffer at least one accident; sustained safety protocols can avoid it. The accident is produced by the factory, not scheduled because the story needs a crisis.
causes: Pressure, room staffing, wear, supervisor decisions and safety practices establish risk. Damage persists before engineering arrives; later, deferred engineering work also matters. Severity includes bounded randomness within those conditions.
Workers and equipment can suffer grave harm. Accidents can repeat if their causes remain or recovery creates new pressures; a second incident also tests earlier promises.

The responsible supervisor experiences stress and a change in confidence. Their account of their responsibility can differ from the physical record. Others form their own views from what reaches them.

The daily consultation can assign blame, relieve self-doubt, reassure with conditions or exploit the incident for another agenda. Orders, resources and later follow-through determine what those words mean.

Choose which supervisors and workers to inform, when, and how to frame the account. Witnesses already know something; repair needs, absences and personal contacts can carry information outside the official account.
accident.disclosure: Disclosure and the private response are separate choices. A director can publicly acknowledge an accident while privately scapegoating someone, or support the supervisor while keeping other rooms uninformed. Neither secrecy nor eventual exposure is guaranteed.
accident.feedback: Damage reduces capacity → quota pressure increases → stressed supervisors interpret the next problem through the accident and the director’s response → their actions change safety and reporting → further incidents or recovery follow. Information can carry this pressure into rooms untouched by the original damage.
accident.guardrail: Safety paths must still reach Brain 2.0. No unlock should require a casualty. Reduced risk must matter across runs; random severity must not routinely overwhelm preparation. Most serious consequences redirect the run, while destruction or exhausted recovery can still end it.
accident.visibility: Show warnings before exposure, a prompt physical result after the decision, and later behavioural echoes. The player may misread a motive, but should be able to learn which operating choices changed risk.

bdi.title: Beliefs, desires and intentions
bdi.intro: Supervisors act on an incomplete interpretation of the factory, their colleagues and their boss. BDI connects that interpretation to a persistent course of action, then lets the result change what they believe next.
triad: “The director says safety matters, but punishes every stoppage.” Store the claim, its source, certainty and contradictory evidence separately from world truth.
What I want to achieve or protect
Meet the quota, keep workers alive, prove competence, protect a colleague or avoid replacement. Several concerns can conflict.
What I have committed to doing
After engineering unlocks: “Keep the line stopped until the repair is verified.” An intention has a plan, a reason to persist and conditions for finishing, abandoning or reconsidering it.
bdi.state: Stress, self-confidence, loyalty, personality, capability and remembered experiences shape interpretation and priorities. They are not three extra names for BDI. Confidence in a particular belief is also distinct from confidence in oneself.
loop: Observe
Receive only available signals and messages. Missing information stays missing.
Interpret
Revise beliefs about the equipment, other people and the director’s expectations.
Prioritize
Weigh competing concerns through personality, stress, history and existing promises.
Commit
Select or retain a plan; record why alternatives were rejected.
Attempt
Request a concrete action. Resolve it against actual equipment, resources and other actions.
Remember
Record the result, revise self-confidence and stress, and decide what to tell whom. That message enters another agent’s observations.
bdi.persistence: Reconsider on relevant new evidence, a changed order, an impossible plan, accumulated strain or a broken promise. Do not choose a fresh personality every shift. Persistence can be useful commitment or harmful fixation, depending on what the supervisor believes.
bdi.ambiguity: A supervisor can sincerely obey a misunderstood order. The player then interprets the supervisor through incomplete reports. Both sides can be wrong without either deliberately lying.
modes: Pursue the director’s perceived priority. A damaging result can come from a mistaken belief about what was required.
Choose an unrequested plan believed to help. Competence, authority and knowledge determine whether it helps.
Protect reputation, a colleague or a principle. That concern can coexist with loyalty and production goals.
Intend to obstruct or damage a particular goal. Require that intent and an available means; do not infer it from a bad outcome.

Accumulated strain disrupts execution or deliberation: fixation, withdrawal, contradictory commands or failed follow-through. Specify the mechanism and recovery; do not roll a random villain personality.

example.title: The same accident, three responses
